newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia's Tudjman sees growth over 7 pct this year.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's Tudjman sees growth over 7 pct this year.

text.p: Croatia's President Franjo Tudjman said on Monday the country's planned reconstruction and tourist expansion could propel economic growth to over seven percent in 1996 and the next few years.
"Croatia is becoming a big building site with large-scale reconstruction projects in liberated areas," Tudjman said in opening remarks at the international autumn trade exhibition.
"A successful tourist season and other favourable international conditions guarantee a real economic growth at annual rates exceeding seven percent this year and in the coming years."
He said Croatia had raked in almost $2.0 billion in hard currency from tourism this year as foreign visitors returned, but that was still less than the best pre-1991 war levels.
However, he predicted the tourist earnings could "double or even treble in the coming years."
There are no growth statistics yet for this year, but Croatia's gross domestic product (GDP) was officially forecast to rise between five and seven percent in real terms.

Independent analysts put the GDP growth at a more modest 4-5 percent, taking into account an expected industrial output recovery, an increase in public sector activities and tourist trade, with a related effect on other businesses.
Tudjman described the current situation and the prospects for further economic development as "very favourable" thanks to a steady industrial output rise in the past 11 months.

"Compared to August last year, the growth totalled 7.6 percent, or 3.7 percent more than what Croatia inherited from (former) Yugoslavia...," he said, citing a strong recovery in shipbuilding, construction, wood-processing and textile industries.
The last set of official figures put the industrial output rise for July at 6.4 percent year-on-year.
Tudjman said the government's efforts to overhaul ailing banks could help spur a new development cycle with radically lower interest rates for the economy and population.

"This will enable larger loans and new investments into production and other businesses, which means opening new jobs and improving the living standard." -- Kolumbina Bencevic, Zagreb Newsroom, 385-1-4557075
